newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: COSTLY S. AFRICAN MINISTRY ADVISERS IN SPOTLIGHT.
newsitem.headline: COSTLY S. AFRICAN MINISTRY ADVISERS IN SPOTLIGHT.

text.p: The South African government is reviewing the position of 45 state-funded ministerial advisers earning up to 345,000 rand a year, controversial Home Affairs Ministry adviser Mario Ambrosini said on Monday.
Ambrosini was grilled for almost two hours by parliament's committee on home affairs over his salary and expenses totalling more than 1.2 million rand since the transition to democracy in 1994.
He said he acted as a personal adviser to Home Affairs Minister and Inkatha Freedom Party leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi and was not accountable to parliament.
"Your problem is that I am paid by Home Affairs, but I don't work for Home Affairs," he said.

But he added that he was aware of controversy about his position, which is widely regarded as that of a state-funded political adviser to Inkatha, the main black rival of President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC).
"The cabinet has indicated that the present system of advisers needs to be changed and the Department of Public Service has been asked to prepare a bill to address the problems," he said.
Nicholas Haysom, Mandela's legal adviser, said he was aware of a proposal to the cabinet to enact measures to govern the work of advisers, but said he was not aware of a final outcome.
A Public Service Ministry spokeswoman said Minister Zola Skweyiya was satisfied with the regulations covering the two advisers allowed for each minister and provincial premier.
The scrutiny of Ambrosini's expenses comes amid rising concern about the army of state consultants and advisers said to cost the government more than one billion rand a year.

The Department of State Expenditure and the Auditor General's office warned legislators earlier this month that there was inadequate financial control over an estimated 2,359 consultants and 562 advisers and information officers.
Consultants and advisers work on contract and are neither paid nor appointed according to standard civil service rules.
Ambrosini, a United States citizen with a heavy Italian accent, has been a key Inkatha adviser since talks on a transition from white rule to democracy started in 1990.
Inkatha sources told Reuters that party members blamed Ambrosini for most of the hawkish positions taken by Buthelezi, often at the cost of participation in transitional structures.
Ambrosini denied that he was involved in party politics, saying it was his job to advise Buthelezi on a wide range of political issues, but not the affairs of Inkatha.
He compared his position to that of 44 other ministerial advisers including Haysom, who assists Mandela and the ANC.
Haysom confirmed that he worked for the ANC, mainly on constitutional issues, but added:

"It is a matter of record that I undoubtedly put in more than eight hours of work a day in the President's office, dealing with run of the mill issues before the President, the cabinet or the government."
Ambrosini said he worked 16 hours a day, seven days a week and that it was almost all in the interests of the country.
He said press scrutiny of his expenses was part of a campaign to undermine Buthelezi.
